newsitem.title: BELGIUM: No early deal seen on EU gene-modified food label.
newsitem.headline: No early deal seen on EU gene-modified food label.

text.p: Efforts to agree labelling rules for genetically modified foods such as Monsanto's "Roundup Ready" soybeans look unlikely to produce an early deal, a European Union diplomat told Reuters on Thursday.

"It looks very difficult because both sides are stuck to their positions," the diplomat said in reference to ongoing talks between EU country officials and members of the European Parliament (Euro-MPs).
Officials from the 15 EU countries met on Wednesday to discuss tactics for next Monday's meeting with Euro-MPs but failed to work out a deal which was likely to break the deadlock, the diplomat said.
Discussions concern which gene-altered foods, in raw or processed form, should be labelled and what information those labels should carry.

Euro-MPs want labels to tell consumers of all the properties that distinguish so-called novel foods from existing equivalent foods or ingredients while EU country officials say such detail is warranted only where there are "significant" differences.

Suggested wording in a Dutch-brokered compromise proposing that food be labelled if its gene modifications were "analytically provable" had not figured during discussions on Wednesday, the diplomat said.

European environmental groups and consumers have grown increasingly sensitive to possbile risks related to the genetic engineering of foods, many of which developers and many governments have said are safe.

The issue has been brought to the fore in recent months by the imminent arrival in Europe of imports from this year's U.S. soybean harvest containing gene-modified soybeans developed by U.S. chemical company Monsanto.
Monsanto's beans are resistant to its "Roundup" herbicide.

Genetic modification of organisms is a term which describes a huge variety of techniques, practised in many industries, to change the biological make-up of plants and animals. This includes the development of new plant strains to be resistant to particular pests or crop chemicals.
